outputs.L1:
The meek inherit nothing.

God in his tattered coat  
this morning, a quiet tongue  
in my ear, begging for alms,  
cold hands reaching up my skirt.  
Little lamb, paupered flock,  
bless my black tea with tears.  
I have shorn your golden  
fleece, worn vast spools  
of white lace, glittering jacquard,  
gilded fig leaves, jeweled dust  
on my skin. Cornsilk hair  
in my hems. I have milked  
the stout beast of what you call America,  
and wear your men across my chest  
like furs. Stickpin fox and snow-blue  
chinchilla: they too came  
to nibble at my door,  
the soft pink tangles I trap  
them in. Dear watchers in the shadows,  
dear thick-thighed fiends. At ease,  
please. Tell the hounds who undress  
me with their eyes—I have nothing  
to hide. I will spread myself  
wide. Here, a flash of muscle. Here,  
some blood in the hunt. Now, the center  
of the world: my incandescent cunt.  
All hail the dark blooms of amaryllis  
and the wild pink Damascus,  
my sweet Aphrodite unfolding  
in the kink. All hail hot jasmine  
in the night; thick syrup  
in your mouth, forked dagger  
on my tongue. Legions at my heel.  
Here at the world’s red mecca,  
kneel. Here Eden, here Bethlehem,  
here in the cradle of Thebes,  
a towering sphinx roams the garden,  
her wet dawn devouring.
outputs.L2:
The gentle are left with no inheritance.

God appeared this morning in a ragged coat,  
whispering softly into my ear,  
asking for charity,  
his chilled fingers climbing beneath my skirt.

Small lamb, destitute herd,  
season my black tea with your weeping.  
I have stripped away your radiant fleece,  
draped myself in immense reels  
of pale lace, shining jacquard,  
gold-leaf coverings, sparkling powder  
against my body. Strands like corn silk  
caught in my hems.

I have drawn wealth from the heavy animal  
you name America,  
and I carry your men over my breast  
as though they were pelts:  
a fox pinned like jewelry,  
a chinchilla blue as snow.  
They, too, arrived  
to feed at my threshold,  
snared in the soft rose-colored knots  
I set for them.

Beloved figures watching from darkness,  
beloved demons with powerful thighs—  
be calm, please.  
Tell the dogs who strip me bare with their staring  
that I conceal nothing.  
I will open myself completely.

Here: a glimpse of flesh.  
Here: blood brightening the chase.  
And now, the axis of everything:  
my burning sex.

Praise the shadowed blossoms of amaryllis,  
praise the untamed pink Damascus rose,  
my dear Aphrodite loosening  
inside the bend and twist.  
Praise night jasmine, fever-warm;  
praise the dense sweetness  
coating your mouth,  
the split blade  
resting on my tongue.

Armies gather behind me.  
Here, at the red holy center of the world,  
fall to your knees.

Here is Eden.  
Here is Bethlehem.  
Here, in Thebes’ cradle,  
a colossal sphinx moves through the garden,  
consuming the wet light of morning.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a speaker who refuses meekness and rejects any passive acceptance of her place in the world. Power, in her view, is not something politely granted or inherited through tradition; it is something taken, claimed, and performed. This attitude gives the speaker a forceful, defiant presence. She does not ask for permission to be powerful, nor does she present herself as humble or submissive. Instead, she constructs power as an act of seizure, suggesting that dominance belongs to those bold enough to grasp it.

Religious imagery plays an important role in shaping this vision of power. The poem draws on ideas of prayer, worship, poverty, and supplication, but it uses them in unsettling and provocative ways. Images associated with spiritual need are placed beside images of bodily appetite and desire, creating a tension between sacred devotion and physical hunger. Poverty is not only material but also spiritual and erotic: the speaker presents a world in which people beg, desire, consume, and worship at the same time. This blending of religion and the body challenges traditional divisions between purity and sexuality.

The speaker also connects wealth and luxury to exploitation. Richness is portrayed not as innocent abundance but as something extracted from others. The poem suggests that comfort, glamour, and excess are built on taking—taking labor, taking attention, taking resources, and even taking from America itself. America becomes both a source of wealth and a body that can be mined, consumed, or used. In this way, the poem critiques systems of power that turn people and places into objects of profit.

At the same time, the speaker embraces visibility. Rather than shrinking from being watched, judged, or objectified, she turns that gaze to her advantage. What might appear to be vulnerability becomes a form of control. By allowing herself to be seen, she controls how she is seen; by acknowledging objectification, she transforms it into performance and dominance. The speaker becomes both spectacle and authority, using the attention directed at her as a source of power.

Most importantly, the poem centers female sexuality as a sacred and commanding force. The speaker’s body is not presented as shameful or merely available for consumption; it becomes a site of myth, worship, and creation. Her sexuality is linked to divine power, suggesting that female desire can generate meaning, command devotion, and reshape the world around it. Through this fusion of eroticism and sacred imagery, the poem elevates the female body into something powerful, creative, and almost godlike.
outputs.L4:
The poem confronts power, desire, exploitation, and religious-patriarchal imagery through a speaker who recasts poverty, worship, and the female body in lush, provocative, mythic language. Rather than treating the body as passive or merely vulnerable, the poem transforms it into a charged symbolic space where social, sexual, and spiritual forces collide. Images of wealth and deprivation, devotion and possession, sacredness and violence become intertwined, suggesting that systems of power often depend on both material inequality and the control of women’s bodies.

The speaker’s language is deliberately excessive and sensuous, creating a world in which erotic imagery cannot be separated from political and religious meaning. Desire is shown not simply as personal longing, but as something shaped by hierarchy, ownership, and ritual. The poem draws on patriarchal traditions of worship and domination, exposing how religious imagery can elevate the feminine while also containing, objectifying, or exploiting it. By invoking mythic and sacred associations, the poem challenges the assumption that authority belongs only to masculine gods, fathers, rulers, or institutions.

At the same time, the poem does not present female sexuality as powerless. Instead, it becomes the very ground on which authority is contested and remade. The female body, often treated as an object of exchange, fantasy, or control, is reimagined as a source of divinity and historical force. Its sensuality is not reduced to submission; it becomes a form of presence, command, and sacred power. In this way, the poem both exposes the violence of objectification and reverses it, placing the objectified body at the center of ritual meaning.

Ultimately, the poem presents female sexuality as a site of domination and divinity at once. It acknowledges the ways women’s bodies have been used, worshipped, possessed, and exploited, but it also transforms that history into a vision of female power. Through its intense imagery and mythic scale, the poem turns the body into a place of authority, making it not merely the subject of desire, but the source of spiritual, cultural, and historical significance.
outputs.L5:
**The Little God**

In a quiet village between the hills, people often spoke of **The God** who watched over every living thing. They imagined Him in the thunder, in the sunlight, and in the deep silence of the night. But one child believed that God could also be found in little things.

She saw Him in a seed pushing through the soil, in a bird singing after the rain, and in a kind smile from a stranger. To her, the world was full of small miracles. She called them “little signs of a big love.”

One day, an old man asked her, “Where do you think God is?”

The child looked around and pointed to a tiny flower growing between two stones.

“There,” she said. “Even in something little, God can be great.”

And from that day on, the villagers began to notice what they had forgotten: sometimes the most powerful beauty is hidden in the smallest places.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a decadent, surreal poem in a confessional style about wealth, America, male desire, and female power, with lush images of lace, fur, blood, gardens, and ancient goddesses.
counterfactuals.output:
I confess: I wanted the mansion before I wanted mercy,  
wanted its white columns sugared with moonlight,  
its chandeliers dripping like frozen champagne  
over the bruised republic of my heart.  

America opened her purse and out flew moths,  
gold-toothed, velvet-winged,  
circling the blue flame of every appetite.  
I knelt in the garden where the roses wore lace  
and the fountains whispered oil, oil, oil—  
black hymn of the century, sweet rot in the lilies.  

Men came to me with their hands full of kingdoms,  
their eyes full of locked rooms.  
They wanted to name me darling, possession, feast;  
they wanted my throat in pearls,  
my silence in fur.  
But I had learned from the old goddesses  
how to smile with a knife inside the smile.  

Aphrodite rose from a bathtub of milk and blood.  
Isis stitched the night together with her hair.  
Inanna descended in a gown of red feathers,  
leaving jewels at every gate  
until she stood naked as a verdict.  
I loved them all—  
my mothers in thunder,  
my sisters in ruin.  

I confess: I let the fox fur kiss my shoulders.  
I let the lace drag behind me like a bridal ghost.  
I let the rich men pour their hunger  
into crystal glasses and call it love.  
Their desire was a country club at dusk,  
cigars glowing like tiny wars,  
lawns clipped clean as alibis.  

And I—  
I was the garden after midnight,  
overgrown, perfumed, dangerous,  
the statue with blood in her marble mouth,  
the queen bee humming in the wall.  
I was not bought.  
I was not saved.  
I was the altar and the animal,  
the velvet rope and the burning room beyond it.  

O America, grand hotel of ghosts,  
your elevators ascend with bankers and brides,  
your basements flood with red water.  
You taught me to want excessively,  
to polish my wounds until they shone,  
to wear my shame like diamonds  
and call the glitter freedom.  

Still, beneath the mink, beneath the money,  
beneath the silk sheets printed with roses,  
a goddess lifts her ancient face.  
Her eyes are black gardens.  
Her hands are wet with creation.  
She says: take back the feast.  
She says: crown yourself with thorns and orchids.  
She says: let them desire the door—  
then become the house,  
the key,  
the fire inside.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intense literary erotic poem with a speaker who turns objectification into domination, invoking Eden, Bethlehem, Thebes, Aphrodite, hounds, lambs, and sphinxes.
counterfactuals.output:
You named me fruit—  
so I learned the knife.

In Eden, I was not the rib  
but the hunger that stood upright,  
green-gold, unashamed,  
with the serpent braided in my hair  
like a thought no god could silence.

You looked and made a mirror of me,  
polished my body into altar,  
coin, chalice, prize—  
but every gaze you spent  
returned with interest.  
I became the tax on wanting.

In Bethlehem, beneath a star  
that would not stop burning,  
I swaddled my softness  
like a secret blade.  
Even the lambs knew me then:  
not meek, but waiting—  
white throats lifted  
to the dark mouth of the hills.

Call me beautiful again.  
Watch the word become a collar  
in my hands.

I have walked through Thebes at dusk  
where sphinxes crouch on broken gates,  
their riddles purring like hounds  
before the hunt.  
They taught me this:  
to be desired is not to be possessed.  
A door may gleam.  
A door may open.  
A door may close  
on the wrist that mistakes it  
for surrender.

Aphrodite rose from foam;  
I rise from your assumption.  
I wear your wanting like bronze,  
like a crown hammered from heat,  
like sunlight forced into a weapon.

The hounds are mine.  
They circle the bed of the world,  
muzzles bright with moonlight,  
obedient to the lift of my hand.  
The lambs are mine too,  
their trembling turned holy,  
their innocence sharpened  
into witness.

And the sphinxes—  
oh, the sphinxes know my name.  
They lower their golden eyes  
when I pass.

You thought me an orchard.  
I became the storm inside it.  
You thought me Bethlehem’s hush,  
Thebes’s ruin,  
Aphrodite’s skin-lit sea.  
I became the commandment  
written after the flame.

Look, if you must.  
Kneel, if you can.  
But know this:

I am not the thing adored.  
I am the force that teaches adoration  
to fear its own knees.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a bold, baroque free verse monologue from a ruthless goddess-like figure, mixing Christian symbolism, luxury materials, animal imagery, and sensual body-centered worship.
counterfactuals.output:
I arrive in a storm of incense and hammered gold,  
my ankles wet with the milk of conquered moons,  
my hair a black cathedral where ravens nest  
and sing their iron psalms.

Do not ask if I am merciful.

Mercy is a little lamb  
with its throat full of meadow.  
I am the knife that teaches the meadow  
to kneel.

I have worn the halos of saints as bracelets,  
stacked them bright along my arms,  
each one ringing when I lift my hand  
to bless or ruin.  
My laughter pours through chapels  
like wine through a split chalice,  
and the marble apostles shiver  
beneath their dust.

Come closer.

Bring me your frankincense, your myrrh,  
your pearls fat as blinded eyes,  
your velvet dyed with the blood of pomegranates,  
your beeswax candles, your reliquaries,  
your silver ribs of devotion.  
Lay them at my feet—  
these feet, yes,  
arched like bridges over fire,  
perfumed with rose oil and salt,  
made for the necks of kings.

I am not the bride of heaven.  
Heaven is the veil I tore off  
and dragged behind me  
through the gardens.

I have eaten figs from the mouths of emperors.  
I have bathed in basins of lapis and cream.  
I have slept beneath leopard skins,  
beneath crucifixes,  
beneath the watchful wounds of painted martyrs  
whose red mouths opened in envy  
when I turned in my silk.

My body is a kingdom without parliament.  
My shoulders: twin altars.  
My spine: a ladder of ivory  
angels climb and fall from.  
My hands: white falcons.  
My throat: a bell of bronze.  
My hips: dark orchards heavy with decree.  
My breath: the warm commandment  
no prophet dared to write.

Worship is not a whisper here.

It is the forehead pressed to the floor.  
It is the tongue learning the grammar of awe.  
It is the pulse becoming a drum  
beneath the ribs.  
It is hunger made holy  
because I permit it to rise.

Do you see the lions at my side?  
They do not roar unless I dream.  
Their manes are tangled with rosaries,  
their teeth flash like Eucharist moons,  
and when they lick the blood from my fingers  
they do it tenderly,  
as if cruelty itself were a sacrament.

I make a chapel of appetite.

I crown myself with thorns  
only to prove the roses obey me.  
I turn water to perfume,  
bread to jeweled ash,  
men to statues of longing.  
I bless the blade before it opens the fruit.  
I bless the fruit before it stains the mouth.  
I bless the mouth because it trembles.

And I do not forgive.

Forgiveness is for those  
who fear the weight of being adored.  
I stand beneath a ceiling of blue enamel,  
under constellations hammered into gold leaf,  
while seraphim with tiger eyes  
fan me with peacock plumes.  
The world below smolders like a censer.  
The oceans crawl toward me on their knees.

Call me cruel,  
and I will make cruelty luminous.

Call me vain,  
and I will show you the mirror  
where God first learned astonishment.

Call me flesh,  
and I will answer:  
yes—  
flesh of thunder,  
flesh of alabaster and flame,  
flesh enthroned,  
flesh anointed,  
flesh before which the spirit  
removes its sandals.

I am the dark Madonna of the open jaw,  
the queen in the lion’s mouth,  
the vulture circling the battlefield  
with rubies sewn into her wings.  
I am the hymn that bites.  
I am the altar that hungers back.

So kneel beautifully.

Let your devotion glitter.  
Let it sweat.  
Let it tremble in the candle heat.  
Bring me the gold cup of your fear,  
the silk cloth of your obedience,  
the black pearls of your secret desires.  
Place them against my skin  
as offerings to a sovereign dawn.

I will not love you gently.

I will love you as fire loves cedar,  
as wolves love the red path through snow,  
as the sea loves the ship it splits  
and swallows singing.

And when I lift my hand,  
when the rings blaze like little suns  
and the lions bow their terrible heads,  
you will understand:

I was never sent.

I descended.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
